summary.text: Assuming the claimed additive identity, the shifted terms \(a_n+1\) follow the Fibonacci transition; a matrix-power computation modulo \(p=195318521017\), starting from the actual terms at indices 3773 and 3774, shows that \(p\) divides both \(a_{249580077006}\) and \(a_{249580077007}\). Agreement of the defining recurrence with the claimed identity at the next index forces these two positive consecutive terms to have gcd \(1\), contradicting their common divisor \(p>1\).

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\geq 1}\) be the sequence defined by
\[
a_1=a_2=1,
\qquad
a_n=d_n+\frac{a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}}{d_n}\quad(n\geq3),
\qquad
d_n=\gcd(a_{n-1},a_{n-2}).
\]
We disprove the conjecture by showing that its first asserted identity cannot hold for every \(n\geq3775\). Since the full conjecture asserts that identity together with two others, this suffices to disprove the entire conjunction.

Assume for contradiction that
\[
a_n=1+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}                         \tag{1}
\]
for every \(n\geq3775\).

Define the shifted terms
\[
b_n=a_n+1.
\]
Equation (1) implies
\[
b_n=a_n+1=2+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}=b_{n-1}+b_{n-2}  \tag{2}
\]
for every \(n\geq3775\). Thus, under the conjectured identity, the shifted sequence follows the ordinary Fibonacci recurrence from this point onward.

We now give the finite modular computation used to reach the contradiction. Set
\[
m=195318521017,
\qquad
q=249580073233,
\qquad
T=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Direct calculation of the defining gcd recurrence through index \(3774\), retaining the integer terms themselves while calculating each gcd, gives
\[
a_{3773}+1\equiv77940394259\pmod m,
\qquad
a_{3774}+1\equiv99768150822\pmod m.          \tag{3}
\]
For completeness, this finite calculation can be reproduced starting with \(x=y=1\), and for \(n=3,4,\ldots,3774\) replacing the pair \((x,y)=(a_{n-2},a_{n-1})\) by
\[
\left(y,\ \gcd(x,y)+\frac{x+y}{\gcd(x,y)}\right).
\]
After the last step one reduces the entries at indices \(3773\) and \(3774\), after adding \(1\), modulo \(m\). The terms involved have only 340 or 341 decimal digits, so this is an ordinary finite sequence of Euclidean-algorithm and integer-division calculations. As an additional check on the indexing, the same calculation gives
\[
a_{3772}+1\equiv21827756563\pmod m.
\]

A modular repeated-squaring calculation gives
\[
T^q\equiv
\begin{pmatrix}
117378126758&21827756563\\
21827756563&139205883321
\end{pmatrix}
\pmod m.                                                    \tag{4}
\]
This matrix calculation is readily reproducible without handling enormous Fibonacci numbers. One may use
\[
T^r=\begin{pmatrix}F_{r-1}&F_r\\F_r&F_{r+1}\end{pmatrix}
\]
for \(r\geq1\), together with the doubling formulas
\[
F_{2r}=F_r(2F_{r+1}-F_r),
\qquad
F_{2r+1}=F_r^2+F_{r+1}^2,
\]
reducing after every operation modulo \(m\). Reading
\[
q=(11101000011100001000011011000100010001)_2
\]
by binary exponentiation yields
\[
F_q\equiv21827756563,
\qquad
F_{q+1}\equiv139205883321\pmod m.
\]
Consequently
\[
F_{q-1}=F_{q+1}-F_q\equiv117378126758\pmod m,
\]
which is exactly (4).

Multiplying the matrix in (4) by the vector from (3) gives
\[
T^q
\begin{pmatrix}a_{3773}+1\\a_{3774}+1\end{pmatrix}
\equiv
\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}\pmod m.                  \tag{5}
\]
Here the two unreduced integer dot products, which make the final modular reduction explicit, are
\[
\begin{aligned}
&117378126758\cdot77940394259
 +21827756563\cdot99768150822\\
&\hspace{35mm}=11326212385784681827108
 =57988419771\,m+1,
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
&21827756563\cdot77940394259
 +139205883321\cdot99768150822\\
&\hspace{35mm}=15589577514788957011679
 =79816176334\,m+1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus both coordinates really are congruent to \(1\) modulo \(m\).

We next connect this finite computation with the assumed formula. The transition matrix satisfies
\[
T\begin{pmatrix}u\\v\end{pmatrix}
 =\begin{pmatrix}v\\u+v\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Using (2), an induction on \(k\geq0\) therefore gives
\[
T^k\begin{pmatrix}b_{3773}\\b_{3774}\end{pmatrix}
 =\begin{pmatrix}b_{3773+k}\\b_{3774+k}\end{pmatrix}.       \tag{6}
\]
Indeed, the assertion is immediate when \(k=0\). If it holds for \(k\), multiplication by \(T\) changes the right-hand vector to
\[
\begin{pmatrix}b_{3774+k}\\b_{3773+k}+b_{3774+k}\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}b_{3774+k}\\b_{3775+k}\end{pmatrix},
\]
where the last equality is (2), applicable because \(3775+k\geq3775\). This is the assertion for \(k+1\).

Take \(k=q=249580073233\) in (6). Since
\[
3773+q=249580077006,
\qquad
3774+q=249580077007,
\]
equation (5) implies
\[
b_{249580077006}\equiv1\pmod m,
\qquad
b_{249580077007}\equiv1\pmod m.
\]
Recalling that \(b_n=a_n+1\), we obtain
\[
m\mid a_{249580077006}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
m\mid a_{249580077007}.                                  \tag{7}
\]
Thus the assumed Fibonacci behavior forces two consecutive terms of the original sequence to have the nontrivial common divisor \(m\).

It remains to show that the defining recurrence and the conjectured recurrence instead force these same two terms to be coprime. We first establish the elementary fact needed for this.

Suppose \(x,y\) are positive integers and put \(d=\gcd(x,y)\). If
\[
d+\frac{x+y}{d}=1+x+y,                                  \tag{8}
\]
then \(d=1\). To see this, since \(d\) divides both \(x\) and \(y\), it divides \(x+y\); write
\[
r=\frac{x+y}{d}.
\]
Equation (8) becomes
\[
d+r=1+dr,
\]
or equivalently
\[
(d-1)(r-1)=0.                                             \tag{9}
\]
Moreover, because \(x,y>0\) and \(d=\gcd(x,y)\), one has \(d\leq x\) and \(d\leq y\). Hence
\[
x+y\geq2d,
\qquad	ext{so}\qquad r=\frac{x+y}{d}\geq2.
\]
Thus \(r-1\neq0\), and (9) forces \(d-1=0\), proving \(d=1\).

Now abbreviate
\[
N=249580077006,
\qquad
x=a_{N+1}=a_{249580077007},
\qquad
y=a_N=a_{249580077006}.
\]
The numbers \(x\) and \(y\) are positive. For example, applying the assumed identity (1) at indices \(N\) and \(N+1\), both of which are at least \(3775\), writes each as \(1\) plus two nonnegative integers.

At index \(N+2=249580077008\), the actual defining recurrence says
\[
a_{N+2}=\gcd(x,y)+\frac{x+y}{\gcd(x,y)}.                  \tag{10}
\]
On the other hand, the assumed conjectural identity (1), applied at the same index, says
\[
a_{N+2}=1+x+y.                                            \tag{11}
\]
Equating (10) and (11), the elementary result just proved yields
\[
\gcd(x,y)=1.                                               \tag{12}
\]

But (7) says that \(m\) divides both \(x\) and \(y\). Therefore \(m\) divides \(\gcd(x,y)\). By (12), this says \(m\mid1\), which is impossible because
\[
m=195318521017>1.
\]
This contradiction proves that the identity
\[
a_n=1+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}
\]
cannot hold for every \(n\geq3775\). Consequently, the stated conjecture—which requires this identity and the other two displayed formulas simultaneously for every \(n\geq3775\)—is false.
